rewrites.prompt: A Rundu hardware store sells 50 bags of cement a day, its supplier takes 4 days to deliver, and it keeps 100 bags in reserve. Explain the difference between the store's buffer inventory and its re-order level.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Buffer inventory is a reserve the business intends not to use, held to cover a heavier draw or a late delivery; the re-order level is the trigger at which the next order is placed. The store's buffer is its 100 bags. Its re-order level is higher, because it must also cover what the store expects to sell while the order is on its way: 50 bags a day for 4 days is 200 bags, plus the 100-bag buffer, gives a re-order level of 300 bags. So a longer delivery time would raise the re-order level while leaving the buffer unchanged.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - a reserve not meant to be used against a trigger point for ordering.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the store - a 100-bag buffer against a re-order level of 300 bags, using the formula that links them; 1 mark if the difference is asserted without the store's figures.
Boundary: reserve against trigger, linked by the formula.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Windhoek vehicle assembler receives engines from South Africa twice a day, while a Katima Mulilo hardware store keeps three months of stock because its deliveries can take weeks. Explain the difference between just-in-time and just-in-case inventory management, using these two businesses.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Under just in time, materials arrive as they are needed, so almost no inventory is held: the business minimises holding cost and accepts that a disruption reaches production quickly. Under just in case, buffer stocks are held deliberately so that a late delivery or a jump in demand is absorbed, at a higher holding cost. The assembler's twice-daily engine deliveries are just in time, and a delay at the border could stop its line within hours. The Katima Mulilo store's three months of stock is just in case, which suits a business whose deliveries can take weeks. The difference is which cost each has chosen to carry: holding stock, or being without it.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - which cost the business chooses to carry: holding stock or running out.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the assembler and the Katima Mulilo store, with the exposure to disruption on each side; 1 mark if only one is applied.
Boundary: the chosen cost, not tidiness or modernity.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A manufacturer's inventory falls into three types. Identify each type and give one example of it.
marking_guidance: One mark-worthy point for each type correctly identified with a fitting example. No mechanism or evaluation is required.
A recall card: it asks for all three types, which the papers ask for one item at a time, so it carries no paper tariff.
rewrites.why: State is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Identify and kept as a recall card with no paper tariff.

prompt_replace: State the daily usage rate, the supplier's lead time and the re-order quantity, and say what each one tells the business.
Identify the daily usage rate, the supplier's lead time and the re-order quantity, and explain what each one tells the business.
rewrites.why: State is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Identify and Explain. Three figures are asked for, so no single paper tariff is claimed.

prompt_replace: State what is wrong with that and correct it.
Explain what is wrong with that statement and correct it.
marking_guidance: The error must be stated before it is corrected.
Both faults must be caught: that some inventory remains, and that one cost falling does not mean total costs fall.
A discrimination card: it corrects a stated error, which the papers do not set as a question, so it carries no paper tariff.
rewrites.why: The prompt instructed with State; reworded to Explain and kept as a discrimination card with no paper tariff.

rewrites.prompt: An Otjiwarongo furniture factory could make 1 000 cabinets a month and makes 600, using 20 employees. Explain the difference between its capacity utilisation and its labour productivity.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Capacity utilisation measures output against the maximum output possible, as a percentage; labour productivity measures output against the labour used, as a quantity per worker. The factory's capacity utilisation is 600 out of 1 000, which is 60%, and its labour productivity is 600 / 20 = 30 cabinets per employee a month. They answer different questions and can move apart: if it added 5 employees and output rose to 750 cabinets, capacity utilisation would rise to 75% while productivity stayed at 30 cabinets per employee.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - output against maximum possible output (a percentage) against output per worker (a quantity).
2 marks (AO2): applied to the factory - 60% utilisation and 30 cabinets per employee, and how the two can move apart; 1 mark if only one measure is worked.
Boundary: both measures named in their own units.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Windhoek retailer is considering paying a Windhoek courier to run its deliveries, and a Namibian bank is considering opening its own processing office in another country. Explain the difference between outsourcing and offshoring, using these two plans.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Outsourcing is about who performs an activity - it is handed to another business; offshoring is about where it is performed - it is moved to another country. The retailer's plan is outsourcing without offshoring: the deliveries go to another business, but they stay in Windhoek. The bank's plan is offshoring without outsourcing: the work moves abroad, but the office is still part of the bank. The two are independent, and a business that handed its call centre to a firm in another country would be doing both.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - who performs the activity against where it is performed.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the two plans - one of each without the other; 1 mark if only one plan is classified.
Boundary: both sides of the difference given; the two are independent.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.
